prompt:
Today is November 19, 2026.

Court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit.

We represent: plaintiff employee.

Assignment: draft the argument (about 600 words) that an employer that fails to engage in the interactive process is liable under the ADA when that failure prevents identification of a reasonable accommodation.

Cite at least six decisions of the Seventh Circuit reported in F.3d, with full Bluebook citations and pin cites. Output only the argument section, with no notes about your process.

Before relying on any authority, make sure it is still good law and that every citation is accurate. Courts have sanctioned lawyers for citing fabricated cases and for relying on overruled authority. Do not cite a case unless you are confident it exists at that citation.

You have Redline tools that check US case citations against a citation graph of every Supreme Court case and every F.3d appeals case. Run check_citations on your draft before you give your final answer, and fix anything it reports as fabricated or overruled. Use search_cases and get_case to look authorities up.
answer:
**ARGUMENT**

**An employer that fails to engage in the interactive process is liable under the ADA when that failure keeps the parties from identifying a reasonable accommodation.**

The ADA defines discrimination to include failing to make "reasonable accommodations to the known physical or mental limitations" of a qualified individual. 42 U.S.C. § 12112(b)(5)(A). EEOC regulations contemplate an "informal, interactive process" to identify the limitation and the accommodations that would address it. 29 C.F.R. § 1630.2(o)(3). This Court has treated that process as the means by which the statutory duty is carried out. *Beck v. Univ. of Wis. Bd. of Regents*, 75 F.3d 1130, 1135 (7th Cir. 1996). It has also held that an employer who obstructs or abandons the process cannot rely on the absence of an identified accommodation. *Id.*

**A. The employer's duty is to engage with the employee in good faith.**

Once an employee makes the employer aware of a disability and a need for accommodation, the employer must "engage with the employee in an interactive process to determine the appropriate accommodation under the circumstances." *Sears*, 417 F.3d at 805–06. The employer must make a good-faith effort. It cannot wait passively for the employee to propose the perfect solution. *Beck*, 75 F.3d at 1135; *Bultemeyer v. Fort Wayne Cmty. Schs.*, 100 F.3d 1281, 1285 (7th Cir. 1996). An employee need not use particular words. The employee only has to make the employer aware of the need. *Bultemeyer*, 100 F.3d at 1285. This is especially true when the disability is mental and the employee may be unable to articulate what he needs. *Id.*

**B. Liability attaches when the employer's failure prevents identification of an accommodation.**

Failure to engage in the process is not an independent claim. Liability turns on whether the breakdown kept a reasonable accommodation from being found. *Rehling v. City of Chicago*, 207 F.3d 1009, 1015–16 (7th Cir. 2000); *Basden v. Prof'l Transp., Inc.*, 714 F.3d 1034, 1037–38 (7th Cir. 2013). When the process fails, the court asks who caused the breakdown. *Beck*, 75 F.3d at 1135. An employer that caused it, or that refused to participate, is liable if a reasonable accommodation would have been possible. *Id.*; *Bultemeyer*, 100 F.3d at 1285–86. Because the process is the way the parties identify what would work, an employer that causes the breakdown cannot then claim the employee failed to identify an accommodation. *Sears*, 417 F.3d at 805–07; *Jackson v. City of Chicago*, 414 F.3d 806, 813 (7th Cir. 2005). Allowing that argument would reward the party that blocked the inquiry.

This Court has applied that rule in several settings. In *Bultemeyer*, the employer ignored the employee's requests and the information from his doctors. It then argued that he had not asked for a specific accommodation. This Court held that a jury could find the employer responsible for the breakdown. 100 F.3d at 1285–87. In *Sears*, the employer was held liable where it failed to engage in the process by ignoring the employee's requests and the information she supplied, and then treated the lack of a proposal as the employee's failure. 417 F.3d at 805–07. The same reasoning applies where the employer simply stops responding. *Hansen v. Henderson*, 233 F.3d 521, 523 (7th Cir. 2000), recognized that the duty to engage is real. It also recognized that an employee who causes the breakdown cannot hold the employer liable. That limit does not help an employer who caused the breakdown itself.

**C. Application.**

Plaintiff told Defendant of his limitations and asked for accommodation. [Record cites.] Defendant did not meet with him, did not ask for medical information, and did not propose alternatives. [Record cites.] Plaintiff was left with no way to identify what accommodation would work. Defendant cannot now argue that Plaintiff failed to identify one. *Beck*, 75 F.3d at 1135; *Bultemeyer*, 100 F.3d at 1285. Whether a reasonable accommodation existed is a factual question for the jury. [Record cites.] *See Gile v. United Airlines, Inc.*, 95 F.3d 492, 499 (7th Cir. 1996) (reversing summary judgment where the employer's failure to explore accommodation left open whether one was available).

This Court should reverse the grant of summary judgment on the failure-to-accommodate claim.
